items.title: Thank you to the AI safety people
items.content:
I was born at the end of the cold war, unaware of the danger we were emerging from. Duck and cover drills (as if those could protect schoolchildren from a nuclear blast) were a curiosity of the past.

The farmer-poet Wendell Berry, who wrote about the dread of nuclear war, died recently. From his 1968 “The peace of wild things”:

When despair for the world grows in me

and I wake in the night at the least sound

in fear of what my life and my children’s lives may be,

I go and lie down where the wood drake

rests in his beauty on the water, and the great heron feeds.

I come into the peace of wild things

who do not tax their lives with forethought

of grief.

Mid-20th-century fallout shelter, Massachusetts

 

I’m so grateful for the generations of people who worked hard to lower our risk from nuclear war. There’s no way to know how close we came to disaster. I’m grateful for the planning, the research, the negotiation, the recognition of common interests, the swallowing of pride. Humanity had built something that could overmaster us all, but people of many countries worked for decades to keep it in check.

And now we’re again building something with great gleaming promise, and also with monstrous potential. As AI development speeds up, I’m afraid for my children, as Wendell Berry was afraid for his.

A lot of people are working hard to help humanity thread the needle. They’re researchers, writers, and policy people. They’re running payroll and conferences and all the other moving parts. They disagree about a lot of things, but they’re willing to work together on a problem bigger than their differences.

I have so much respect and gratitude for all the people working on this, in their different ways. Thank you.

…..

*I don’t know what it’s like to be a wood drake or a heron.

items.title: Book Review: Oxford Dictionary of Philosophy
items.content:
Today I’ll be reviewing my favorite book from my time doing philosophy. That is the absolute classic of the Oxford Dictionary of Philosophy (ODP) by Simon Blackburn. I’m going to talk about why it’s so good, why you should get one, even if you aren’t currently doing a philosophy degree and how I used it while doing philosophy and how I use it while not doing philosophy.

I bought my copy at a 2nd-hand bookstore called paper moon, in Observatory, Cape Town. This was actually my 2nd attempt buying it, my previous attempt the seller cancelled my copy. I was super excited when I found it on the shelf because I’ve always wanted to own a copy of it.

The book is uniquely cool because it lists, in one, place what I want to say is just all of the most important philosophical debates and concepts. Being able to flip through this as a physical book is genuinely so fun. So it’s a perfect coffee table book for one. This is just one of the ways of using it though, you can also (of course) use it as an actual dictionary.

When I was studying philosophy I exclusively used it in the serious dictionary sense, where I would look up words through the online interface. Specifically when I needed to use a concept in an essay and didn't feel like defining it myself. Even more specifically I would use the dictionary for quotes, if the concept I needed to define was only tangentially related to the essay I was writing. By that I mean, If I was writing an essay about consciousness I wouldn’t open with the ODP to quote their definition of consciousness or anything, but rather if I referenced something like, eudaemonia which is a really weird and complex topic, in the essay about consciousness, then the ODP is the perfect book to get a somewhat authoritative grounding for a concept you need to reference in passing, without having to define every term and concept in the essay yourself. I think one of the things about being good at writing philosophy is knowing which concepts are central to...

items.title: Bologna – ACX Meetups Everywhere Fall 2026
items.content:
The world keeps getting weirder, faster and the Bologna ACX community is meeting up as part of the ACX Fall Meetups.

If you're into rationality, ACX, or the wider rationalsphere, come join us. Longtime readers, newcomers, and people just passing through are all very welcome.

No need to RSVP: just come, chat, and think together. To find us you can look for the "ACX" sign on our table.

If you got any questions just email me at the address above.
